In [[aeroacoustics]], '''Lighthill's eighth power law''' states that power of the sound created by a turbulent motion, far from the turbulence, is proportional to eighth power of the characteristic turbulent velocity, derived by [[Sir James Lighthill]] in 1952.<ref>Lighthill, M. J. (1952, March). On sound generated aerodynamically I. General theory. In Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A (Vol. 211, No. 1107, pp. 564–587). The Royal Society.</ref><ref>Lighthill, M. J. (1954, February). On sound generated aerodynamically. II. Turbulence as a source of sound. In Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A (Vol. 222, No. 1148, pp. 1–32).</ref> This is used to calculate the total acoustic power of the [[jet noise]]. The law reads as

:<math>W = K \frac{\rho_o}{c_o^5} L^2 U^8,</math>

where
*<math>W</math> is the acoustic power in the far-field,
*<math>K</math> is the proportionality constant (or Lighthill's constant),
*<math>\rho_o</math> is the uniform fluid [[density]],
*<math>c_o</math> is the [[speed of sound]],
*<math>L</math> is the characteristic length scale of the turbulent source and
*<math>U</math> is the characteristic velocity scale of the turbulent source.

The eighth power is experimentally verified and found to be accurate for low speed flows, i.e., [[Mach number]] is small, <math>M<1</math>. And also, the source has to be compact to apply this law.
